content: Comprehensive treatment approaches that address both medical and psychosocial issues, including peer interventions and integrated care for hepatitis C virus (HCV), can improve patient acceptance, treatment uptake, and adherence. These strategies have been shown to reduce injecting drug use and improve safer injection practices. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidance on brief behavioral interventions for substance use through its ASSIST package. Limited data suggest that people who inject drugs (PWID) treated with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for HCV achieve high sustained virologic response (SVR) rates. However, drug-drug interactions (DDIs) can occur between prescribed and non-prescribed substances. Globally, approximately 10 million individuals are incarcerated at any given time, and HCV infection is more prevalent among incarcerated populations. A meta-analysis reported a global HCV prevalence of 26% among general detainees and 64% among those with a history of injecting drug use. The incidence of HCV infection is estimated at 1.4 per 100 person-years, increasing to 16.4 per 100 person-years in individuals with a history of injecting drug use. Among PWID, 58% have a history of incarceration, and 56–90% are likely to be incarcerated at some point. The criminalization of drug use contributes to the high frequency of HCV in prisons and other closed settings, where one in five prisoners is detained for drug-related offenses. Transmission in these settings is driven by injecting drug use, tattooing, and possibly sexual transmission among men. Despite this, opioid substitution therapy (OST) is available in prisons in only 52 countries, and needle and syringe programs (NSPs) are present in prisons in just eight countries. Prisons present an opportunity to provide prevention, testing, care, and treatment services to marginalized populations who may otherwise face barriers to accessing healthcare. Expanding NSP and OST coverage in prisons is essential. The United Nations 2016 General Assembly Special Session on Drugs emphasized the need for non-discriminatory access to medication-assisted therapy, including in custodial settings, and recommended that national authorities consider implementing NSPs in these environments. The short duration of DAA treatment makes it feasible to deliver in prisons, even through task-sharing with nurses. However, mandatory or coercive testing, segregation of prisoners, and denial of treatment have been reported as negative consequences of testing in prisons. Continuity of care between community and prison settings is critical, as individuals, particularly PWID, often cycle between incarceration and community life. Interruptions in medical care, including OST and treatment for HIV and HCV, frequently occur during incarceration and upon reentry into the community. Indigenous Peoples worldwide are disproportionately affected by viral hepatitis, including HCV. The estimated 370 million Indigenous Peoples face challenges such as displacement, systemic racism, and limited access to healthcare, often exacerbated by the remoteness of their communities and cultural or language barriers. In countries like Canada and Australia, high rates of incarceration and injecting drug use among Indigenous populations further increase their risk of HCV infection. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples emphasizes their right to actively participate in the development and administration of health programs affecting them and to access health services without discrimination. HCV is not commonly transmitted through unprotected sexual intercourse among monogamous heterosexual partners. However, certain sexual practices, such as those causing mucosal trauma, group sex, chemsex (drug use during sex), and co-infection with HIV, increase the risk of sexual transmission of HCV among men who have sex with men (MSM). Non-injecting HIV-infected MSM populations have a high incidence of HCV infection, with risk factors including unprotected receptive anal intercourse, ulcerative sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and low CD4 counts. WHO guidelines recommend regular HCV testing for MSM and providing information on transmission risks during male-to-male sex. Treating HCV-infected MSM with DAAs can prevent onward transmission. Sex workers of all genders are at higher risk of HCV infection due to factors such as higher rates of substance use, injecting drug use, and HIV infection. Strategies to engage sex workers in care include outreach, on-site testing services, peer-based interventions, and linkage to other health and welfare services. Where substance use is present, access to harm reduction interventions such as OST and NSP should be provided.
